In ancient times, the Holy Scripture had, both for the individual and social life of Christians, a value and meaning that modern times are largely unaware of. Christians inherited from the Jews the iconscience of the mysterious treasure of wisdom and love that was enclosed in their venerable and sacred books, the absolute faith in the divinity of their message. The Catholic struggle against its enemies, pagans, schismatics and heretics, still contributed greatly to converting the Bible, not only into a battlehorse, but also into a direct and immediate norm of thought and conduct. The persecution against the Holy Books further favored Christian esteem and veneration towards them. The example of Saint Augustine, although of colossal and exceptional dimensions, will reveal to us the importance that this Sacred Scripture had in the life of the Church and its children. It is often said that Saint Augustine is not a theoretical and abstract biblical scholar, but that he became involved in biblical problems by the force of facts. If this expression is intended to suggest that the events were for him a starting point, a basis, there is nothing to oppose. But if the intention is to suggest that Augustinian's solution to such problems was circumstantial and empirical, an urgent solution without universal value, the expression is false: what is important and significant in Augustinian's work is the theory and abstraction that he managed to elaborate, synthesize and pour into his writings, although he started from facts common to him and his contemporaries. That perennial and valid part forever, that structure of principles, that breath of the spirit that survives all events, is what primarily interests modern man, not the ephemeral and expired part that arose with circumstances, depended on them and with them faded away. Saint Augustine is a child of his time. To judge him in the light of modern standards, as Jülicher does, to present us with a kind of regrettable current biblical scholar, is a manifest injustice. Wouldn't it be unfair to bring Galileo or Aristotle before a tribunal to examine his actions?

What high school subjects? Saint Augustine must be judged in the circumstances that surrounded him and in light of them his personal work must be assessed. But we must also guard against the opposite temptation of identifying Saint Augustine with the modern biblical scholar, because Saint Augustine sometimes orients problems in the sense of modern science. Saint Augustine is frequently cited for or against modern opinions. But modern points of view suppose technical means, working instruments, discoveries, discussions, heresies, progress, excavations, ancient literatures, understanding of the ancient East, of the ancient literary genres, of the methods anciently used in the composition of books, all things that Saint Augustine could not even dream of.
THE PROBLEM OF THE METHOD

In Saint Augustine's first encounter with the Bible he felt disillusioned by that vulgar and naïve style that did not admit of comparison with Ciceronian grandiloquence 1. However, for nine years, that is, from nineteen to twenty-eight of his age, he was a convinced Manichaean and, as such, he dealt intensely with biblical problems, especially in his controversies with Catholics. This fact is of such importance that the positions of the Catholic Augustine cannot be well understood if his previous Manichean positions are not taken into account. We accept Allgeier's words: "in the following pages I am going to demonstrate that Augustine's exegetical problem is well explained by his relationship with Manichaeism... Manichaeism gave a precise direction to his thought and fixed him towards the biblical field without abandoning him throughout his life." 2. Burkitt and Puech point out as a very marked characteristic of Manichaeism the ease with which it adapts to the way of being of the countries in which it spreads. Thus, in North Africa it showed such a close kinship with Christianity, that in a certain way it seemed like a Christian heresy 3, in which the biblical sense typical of the disciples of Bardesanes and Marcion was clearly accused. It is true that they frequently spoke against the Catholic Bible, but their attack was actually directed at hermeneutics, at interpretation, not at the position and value of the Bible itself as a source of revelation. They were, as Mondanon very well says, dogmatists who try to pass themselves off as freethinkers, and who, in spite of themselves, always appear as dogmatists 7. Such admission of dogmatic authority may seem strange in Manichaeism, but it is usually explained by the contagion suffered in their contacts with Gnostic sects and Christian communities. The method was easily converted into doctrine, and thus we see that the Manichaeans intend to discuss metaphysical problems, especially that of good and evil, and from that discussion they intend to deduce the principles of Manichaeism. Everything presents the problem of criteria. There are several specific criteria. Thus, for example, Félix believes, like our Protestants, that the Bible does not need authorities to explain it: Félix dixit: ipsa se Scriptura interpretatur13. Unde ingenti positus aestu, ratione cogebar in alterum e duobus, ut aut falsum pronuntiare capitulum, aut mendacem Christum li. Saint Augustine will reproach them for this attitude: "that is not submitting to the Bible, but rather submitting the Bible to personal whim." 15 But ultimately and truly, the criterion was fides manichaea, a Manichaean creed: whatever contradicts the doctrine of Manes is not the Bible, unless it can be interpreted in Manichean; whatever favors Manes is the Bible: M\e manichaea fides reddidit tutum,16. Although the Manichean, in his debate with the Catholics, takes care to conceal this criterion, since he does not have an uninterrupted and reliable tradition like them, Augustine must have clearly seen the essence of the problem, judging by his way of reacting once converted to Catholicism towards his former coreligionists. As can be seen, the strength of Augustine's Catholic texts against modern Protestantism comes from the fact that the Manichean position was very similar to that of the Protestants. Once submitted to this criterion, the Manichaeans proceed to organize the other problems: they begin by posing a radical antinomy between the Old Testament and the New, as laws of hate and love respectively 17. The authors of the Old Testament must be liars and falsehoods, since they attribute so many crimes to the patriarchs 18, although the patriarchs are heroes worthy of such authors 19. The Old Testament presents us with an ignorant, jealous, cruel, God. bloodthirsty, immoral, fickle, ridiculous 20. That Old Testament contradicts itself, it contradicts reason as well as morality 21. Manichaeism boasted a critical and realistic sense. Although Manichean hermeneutics goes from one extreme to the other, from the rabidly literal interpretation of the Old Testament to the Gnostic commentary of the New, the literal interpretation is the one that dominates in the 3rd system. Some biblical texts are resorted to where the Manichean interpretation finds a more plausible context, or they are simply taken out of their context, and then the pretext is alleged that the other texts cannot contradict them, and that is what Faust of Milevi usually does. But there is a thought that worked deeply for Augustine during his Manichaeism. He expected clear revelations of the truth from the Manichaeans and grew tired of waiting, lamenting that only dogmas were given to him (credere iubebar, cf. supra). He began to suppose that the Manichaeans maintained an esoteric arcana that they would reveal to him later: putabam eos magnum aliquid tegere illis involucris, quod essent aliquando aperturi 3?. In his profession as a rhetorician he understood that just as to interpret Terenciano Mauro it was necessary to consult Asper, Cornuto and Donato, and just as Virgil's love songs to the boy Alexis can be interpreted in a dignified and noble manner, so perhaps the Sacred Books can admit a satisfactory interpretation 3 S.

Saint Augustine does not have a well-defined and detailed theory of inspiration, such as is found in modern authors. It emphasizes the action of God and that of the hagiographer, but does not take care to specify what is to be attributed to one or the other. It never occurred to him that there could be any contradiction between the two factors, since for him it was a specific application of the competition theory in which he never found a contradiction. That is why it is dangerous to take isolated phrases as Augustinian sentences, which are almost always circumstantial, referring to a specific point, to the commentary on a specific text. For this reason, the distinction between inspiration and revelation is not appreciated. This is also why he almost always uses the term "prophecy" to talk about inspiration, relying on a text 38 *, in which Saint Paul calls what we call acceptio rerum "tongues" and intelligence or iudicium de rebus "prophecy." Thus, for example, says Saint Augustine, Pharaoh saw a dream and Joseph understood it: Joseph was inspired, but Pharaoh was not: Ulius spiritus informatus est ut videret; huius mens illuminata ut intelligeret. Saint Augustine confesses that this problem already tormented him during his Manichean youth, when he asked himself: "How do you know that these Books were given to the human race by the Spirit of the one God?" 88. His musings led him to establish tradition as a criterion, with a clarity not known before him. As in all the Fathers, Saint Augustine focuses first on "authenticity" or "canonicity", because only the Bible is owed and paid the absolute homage of faith. And along with canonicity comes inspiration, since considering a book as apostolic or prophetic includes considering it inspired or divine, assuming that the prophets and apostles speak in the name of Christ and under his action 8 U. He wants to see things in a very naive way, imagining that the priests are transmitting the old Scriptures as well as the new ones from hand to hand, and that they meticulously discuss each of the books. Although such a naive opinion cannot be accepted, Augustinian thought is clearly evident. Thus, for example, speaking of the book of Enoch, Saint Augustine does not doubt that Enoch wrote an inspired book, a book that has not been preserved. Instead, an apocryphal book has been preserved under the name of Enoch. Saint Augustine therefore thinks that the Holy Spirit revealed to those who were in charge of maintaining the canon when a book was written under inspiration and when it was written by human diligence. Although the term "reveal" is not taken in its strict and technical meaning, Saint Augustine's opinion is clear to us, although somewhat naive. The problem of the Canon must have interested Augustine in the very days of his Manichaeism, because it was involved in other problems, for example, that of interpolations, that of the admission of apocryphal books and that of canonical books rejected by the Manichaeans. That is why from the days of his conversion he had to face this problem, beginning by pointing out a criterion of canonicity, since the canonical books are the Holy Scripture in particular. We have already talked about this: it is the Church that is called to say which books are specifically inspired by God, the books that make up the Bible, as opposed to free examination or the particular inspiration of the Paraclete of the Manichaeans. In contrast to the canonical books, he speaks of the "apocrypha", books that attempted to be introduced into the Canon, but did not succeed: Castitas canoras non recepit 3. Regarding these apocryphal books, Saint Augustine explains that those who have transmitted to us the authority of the Scriptures through an unequivocal and evident tradition, already doubted their origin. They are, therefore, books that lack canonical and traditional authority 4. He knows that some inspired books have disappeared. He believes, for example, that Enoch wrote an inspired book, since he reads this in the Epistle of Saint Jude, 14, a different book from the apocrypha that runs under his name, and he wonders how it is possible for an inspired book to disappear. This problem is difficult for him, given the rigorous and naive concept he has of the transmission of the Canon itself. And he responds that the transmitters of the tradition distinguished between the private and public authority of the prophets: they only attributed to God what they considered written with public authority, at the service of the Synagogue or the Church 5. On this point their ruling seems to favor those who consider that canonicity consists in an inspired book being born already ordered for the use of the Church, although official admission in the list or Canon is required as an indispensable condition "quoad nos". The lost books were, therefore, private, that is, not intended for the Church, not canonical. Canonicity is presented as an intrinsic quality of the book independent of tradition, but since the criterion of this canonicity is the tradition itself, it will be necessary for it to say which books are canonical and which are not. In this way Saint Augustine also concluded against the Priscillianists, that it is not possible for there to be an inspired and canonical book (endowed with public authority), but preserved only in a discipline of the particular arcana 8. The Canon of Saint Augustine is the current one, the Alexandrian. He took great care to ensure that it was well defined in the days of his priesthood, since he was informed of the difference between that Alexandrian canon and the Eastern Hebrew one 7. His canon is the Italian one, that of Saint Hippolytus, Saint Ambrose, Saint Innocent I 8.

Today we can smile at many of his solutions, but in his time those solutions were up to the task and were feared by heretics and received with joy by Christians. On the other hand, it frequently shows signs of a very realistic sense that, although it does not coincide with modern exegesis, advanced many points that have contributed to arriving at this modern exegesis. His tendency to interpret more and more "to the letter" is observed in the different attempts he made to interpret Genesis. Book III deals with the ambiguity of meaning that Holy Scripture can present. The ambiguity in one's own voices, he tells us, comes either from punctuation or from pronunciation. To avoid these ambiguities, textual criticism must be used, examining the context, comparing the interpreters or resorting to the original. There is also ambiguity coming from taking in its own sense what is written figuratively. The general rule that he proposes to us to dispel this type of ambiguity is that everything in the divine Scripture that cannot refer in the proper sense to the purity of customs or the truth of faith, is considered figurative. From here he goes on to deal with how expressions that indicate some cruelty and yet are attributed to God are to be understood; of the customs of the ancients, which are to be judged by the time in which they lived, not by ours; about how some things are ordered in general and others to specific people, and, therefore, taking this into account, we will be able to resolve many issues that at first glance involve a contradiction. He then points out that the same word does not always mean the same thing; It also tells us that there is no problem in the same passage being understood in several ways, as long as it does not oppose the truth, when what the writer really felt is unknown. 5. The thing to be enjoyed is the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, that is, the Trinity itself. The only and supreme thing pleasing to all, if it can be called a thing, and not rather the beginning of all things, if it can also be called a beginning. Because it is not easy to find a name that can suit so much greatness by which this Trinity can be properly called, except by saying that it is one God of whom, through whom and in whom all things are. Thus the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are, each one of them, God; and the three are one God: likewise each one of them is a complete essence, and the three together are one essence. The Father is neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit; the Son is neither Father nor Holy Spirit; The Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son. The Father is only Father, the Son only Son, and the Holy Spirit only Holy Spirit. All three have the same eternity, the same immutability, the same majesty, the same power. The Father is unity, the Son equality, the Holy Spirit the harmony of unity and equality; These three things are all one through the Father, equal through the Son, and harmonious through the Holy Spirit.

HOW THE WISDOM OF GOD HEALS MAN

13. As cure is the means to heal, so this remedy, that is, the Wisdom of God, took sinners to heal and restore them. And just as the doctor when he bandages the wound does not do it sloppily, but with great care so that the usefulness of the bandage is also accompanied by a certain beauty, so the medicine of Wisdom adapts to our wounds through the taking of man, sometimes healing by means of opposite things and other times by similar things. Just as he who heals the wounds of the body sometimes applies opposite remedies, the cold to the warm, the dry to the moist, and so on; and other times he uses remedies that are similar and, therefore, uses a small round cloth for a round wound, or an elongated piece for an elongated wound, and even he does not use the same ligature for all the members, but adapts the similar one to the similar ones, thus the Wisdom of God to heal man, presented itself in order to heal him; she is the doctor and the medicine. And as the man fell through pride, He used humility to heal him. We were deceived by the wisdom of the serpent, and delivered by the foolishness of God, but what is called wisdom was foolishness to those who despised God, and what is called ignorance is wisdom with which the devil is defeated. We died by using immortality badly, Christ used mortality well so that we may live. The woman having depraved her soul, gave way to illness; With the Vireen's body remaining whole, health sprang forth. The example of the virtues of the Lord also belongs to the same contrary remedies, by whose example vices are cured. Among the similar, which are like bandages for the limbs applied to our wounds, there is having been deceived by the woman and being born from her a man for men, a mortal for mortals, one who with death freed the dead. 21. Furthermore, if it is carefully considered, a man should not even enjoy himself, because no one should love himself for himself, but for the one in whom he should enjoy. Then he is the perfect man, when he directs his entire life towards the immutable life, uniting himself with it with all his affection. If he loves himself for himself, he does not direct himself towards God, since directed towards himself, he distances himself from the immutable. And, therefore, he already enjoys himself with some defect, since man is better when he completely unites himself and embraces the immutable good, than when he distances himself from it to return to himself. Therefore, if you should not love yourself for yourself, but for Him who is the most righteous end of your love, let no other man burn with anger because you also love him, not for him, but for God. God has established this rule of love: you will love, he said, your neighbor as yourself; but to God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your understanding, so that you direct all your thoughts, all your life, all your mind towards him from whom you received the same things that you consecrate to him. When he says: with your heart, with all your soul, with all your understanding, no part of our life omits that it must be exempted from fulfilling this duty to surrender to the joy of another, but rather it commands that everything that was of God be presented to the soul to be loved, as if drawn towards the Good where all the impetus of love is directed. Anyone who loves his neighbor rightly must ensure that he also loves God with all his heart, with all his soul and with all his mind; In this way, loving him as himself, all his love and that of his neighbor directs him to the love of God, whose love does not allow any stream to be born from it that would reduce the flow due to such filtration.

The man judges that he has achieved a great triumph if he manages to dominate his companions, that is, other men; because it is innate to the vicious soul to desire in an extraordinary way and to demand as a due thing what is properly due to the only God. It is iniquitous to want things that are inferior to man to serve him when he does not want to serve what is superior to him; For this reason it was said: He who loves iniquity hates his soul; and from here it comes that the soul becomes weak and sick, and is tormented by the mortal body, because it is necessary that it love it and suffer the consequences of its corruption. When man tries to dominate those who are by nature equal to him, that is, men, this constitutes absolutely intolerable arrogance.

After the resurrection this will take place, so that the body will enjoy absolute vigor and utmost peace while being immortally subject to the spirit; Therefore, care must be taken that this also takes place in the present life, so that the inclination of the flesh changes for the better and thus does not oppose the spirit with disordered movements. Until this is achieved, the flesh desires against the spirit. The spirit does not oppose the flesh because of its "hatred" of it, but because of its dominance, because the more it loves it, the more it wants to have it subject to it, which is better than it. Nor does the flesh confront the spirit out of hatred, but out of the inveterate inclination of bad custom, inherited from our first parents, which has taken root in it as a law of nature. Then what the spirit does by taming the flesh is to break the bonds of bad custom and establish the peace of a good friendship. However, not even those who detest their bodies, deceived by a false opinion, would be ready to lose one eye, even without feeling pain, and even if they had as much insight left in the other as they had with both; unless they are forced to do so by something else that should be preceded. 27. There was no need to give a precept for man to love himself and also his body; What we are and what is inferior to us, as it belongs to us, we love by the inviolable law of nature, which was also enacted in favor of the beasts, because all the beasts destroy themselves and their bodies. It remained for us to be given precepts to love what is above us and what is next to us. The evangelist says: you will love your God and Lord put all your heart, with all your soul and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself. These two precepts include all the law and the prophets. Thus, the end of the precept is love, more doubled, that is, love of God and neighbor. If you understand your whole being, that is, your soul and your body; and the whole being of your neighbor, that is, his soul and his body (man consists of body and soul), you will observe that no type of things that should be loved were omitted in those two precepts. But since the love of God is intimate and the way of loving him appears prescribed, in such a way that all things converge in him, it seems that nothing was said about man's love for himself. But when it is written, you will love your neighbor as yourself, the love that each person should have for themselves does not cease to be intimate at the same time.

l. When writing the previous book on things, I tried to prevent attention not from them, but from what they are, regardless of the fact that they could also mean something else other than them. Now when dealing with signs I warn that no one pay attention to what they are in themselves, but only to what they are signs, that is, to what they symbolize. The sign is anything that, in addition to the physiognomy that it has and presents to our senses, makes something else come to our thoughts. Thus, when we see a footprint we think that an animal passed by and made it; When we see the smoke we know that there is fire underneath; When we hear the voice of an animal we realize the condition of its spirit; When the bugle sounds, the soldiers know if they should advance or retreat or make another movement that the battle demands.

3. Conventional signs are those that all living things give to each other to manifest, as far as possible, the movements of the soul such as sensations and thoughts. We have no other reason to point, that is, to give a sign, but to bring out and transfer to the mind of another what the person who gave such a sign had in his own. Of this class of signs, as far as men are concerned, I have determined to deal and reflect now; because even the signs that have been given to us supernaturally and that are found in the holy Scriptures were communicated to us by those who wrote them. Animals also use this type of signs among themselves by which they manifest the appetite of their soul. The rooster, when he finds food, with the sign of his voice tells the hen to come and eat; The pigeon with its cooing calls to the dove, or, on the contrary, it calls to it; There are many other signs of this kind that can and are usually noticed. It is a question that does not concern the matter we are dealing with whether these signs, such as the countenance and moan of a mourner, spontaneously follow the movement of the soul without the intention of signifying, or are given expressly to signify. As something not necessary, we will omit it in this work.

These twists sometimes do not change the meaning, but they offend those who delight more in things when a certain integrity is maintained in their signs. What is called solecism is nothing more than linking words without that norm with which those who before us, not without authority, spoke the language, coupled them. Thus, for example, it is of no interest to anyone who seeks to know things whether one says Inter homines or inter hominibus, among men. And what is barbarism if not writing a word with different letters or pronouncing it with a different sound than those who spoke Latin before us wrote or pronounced it? He who asks God for forgiveness of his sins cares little which way the word ignoscere, forgive, sounds, whether the third syllable is pronounced long or short. Then what does purity in speech consist of, if not in the observance of another's custom confirmed by the authority of the ancients who spoke the language? 20. This does not happen with that passage of the Apostle: «quod stultum est Dei, sapientius est hominibus, et quod inf; rmum est Dei, fortius est hominibus", what is foolish in God is wiser than men; and what is weak in God is stronger than men; because if anyone had wanted to preserve the Greek construction, saying: «quod stultum est Dei, sapientius est hominum; et quod infirmum est Déi, fortius est hominum", certainly the astute reader would find the true meaning of the sentence; but someone who is duller would not understand, or would understand it poorly. Because such a phrase "sapientius est hominum" is not only vicious in the Latin language, but also ambiguous, since it could be understood that the foolish and weak of men were wiser and stronger than God gives them. However, although the expression "sapientius est hominibus" is not free of ambiguity, it is nevertheless free of solecism. For if it were not for the light that comes from the sentence, it would not appear whether "hominibus" is dative or ablative, coming from the singular "huic homini" or "ab hoc homine." Therefore, it would be better to say "sapientius est quam homines, et fortius est quam homines."

There are also conclusions legitimately deduced from reasoning, which are in themselves false; but that they follow from the error of the one with whom he disputes, which the prudent and learned man deduces, so that, shamed with them by the one whose error they followed, he abandons the error he held, because if he wanted to still remain in it, he would have to admit those conclusions that he condemns. Thus the Apostle did not deduce true conclusions, when he said "not even Christ was raised," and when he said "our preaching is vain, our faith is vain," and all the things that follow there, which are false; because Christ was resurrected, and neither was the preaching of those who announced such things useless, nor was the faith of those who believed them vain. However, these truly false conclusions were deduced from the relationship they had with the sentence of those who affirmed that there was no resurrection of the dead; But once these false propositions are rejected, which would be true if the resurrection of the dead did not occur, the consequence is that the resurrection of the dead occurs.

Therefore, as there is a logical connection, not only between the true conclusions, but also between the false ones, it is easy to learn, even in schools that have nothing to do with the Church, the truth and the logic of the connection. 56. The very truth of connections was not instituted by men, but only warned and noted so that it could be learned and taught, since it is based on the reason of things, which is eternal and instituted by God. Just as he who narrates the order of times does not compose them and he who describes to us the situation of places or the nature of animals, plants and stones, does not demonstrate things instituted by men and he who declares the stars and their movements does not discover anything that has been instituted by him or by any man, in the same way he who says "if the conclusion is false, the premises must be false", says something very true, but he does not make this so, but only declares it. What we previously quoted from the apostle Saint Paul falls under this law. The precedent set by those whose error the Apostle wanted to destroy was that there was no resurrection of the dead. After that premise, by which it was said that the resurrection of the dead did not occur, it was necessarily concluded, "therefore Jesus Christ was not resurrected." This consequence is false, because Jesus Christ was resurrected; Therefore the premise is false; and the premise is, there is no resurrection of the dead; then there is resurrection of the dead. All this is summarized like this: «if there is no resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ was not resurrected; but Christ is risen, therefore there is resurrection of the dead. This natural connection that, once the conclusion is removed, necessarily follows the premise, was not instituted by men, but rather shown. This rule pertains to the truth of the connection, not to the truth of the propositions themselves.

Since the snail does not have a voice, since the consequent is removed, the antecedent is removed, it is concluded that the snail is not an animal. This sentence is false, but the connection of the conclusion, deduced from a falsely admitted premise, is true. Thus, the truth of a proposition or premise depends on itself; The truth of the connection depends on the opinion of the one with whom it is disputed and what he has granted. Therefore, as we said above, we will draw a false consequence with true logic, so that the one whose error we want to correct regrets having granted a premise from which follows a consequence that he must reject. From this it is easily understood that, as there are true conclusions in false sentences, so there can be false conclusions in true sentences. We grant that someone says: "If he is just, he is good," and this is granted; and then he says: "but it is not fair", and granted too, he draws the conclusion: "therefore it is not good." All of these things are certainly true, but the rule of conclusion is not. Because if it is true that removing the consequent necessarily removes the antecedent, it is not true that removing the antecedent the conclusion disappears. And so we have that it is true when we say: "if this man is an orator he is a man"; But if we say of this proposition: "but it is so that he is not an orator," then by removing the antecedent we will not draw the true conclusion by saying: "therefore he is not a man."

SCIENCE OF DEFINE AND DIVIDE IS NOT FALSE, EVEN IF IT APPLIES TO FALSE THINGS. WHAT IS FALSE

53. The science of defining, dividing and distributing, although it is often applied to false things, is nevertheless not false in itself, nor has it been instituted by men, but rather found in the nature of things. Well, not because poets use it in their fables, and false philosophers and heretics, that is, bad Christians, tend to use it in their erroneous opinions, that is why it is false that in the definition, division and distribution what is proper to the same thing must enter, or something that belongs to it must be omitted. This principle of dialectic is true even if the things defined or divided are false. Because the same thing false is also defined when we say "that false is the meaning of a thing that is not as indicated," or another similar definition; whose definition is true, although the false cannot be true. We can also divide the false by saying: that there are two types of falsehoods; one of the things that absolutely cannot exist; another of those that do not exist but could have existed. Thus, he who says seven and three are eleven, affirms what can never be; But he who tells, for example, that it rained on January 1st, even if it did not happen, says something that could have happened. Therefore, the definition of false things can be true, even if what is false is not true.

55. When we learn rhetoric, we should rather use it to explain what we have understood than to understand what we do not know. But once the logic and dialectic taught by the rules of consequences, definitions and distributions are learned, they are very helpful to those who try to learn, as long as they avoid the error of those who think that having learned these arts they are already in possession of the same truth that leads to eternal life. Well, it often happens that men achieve more easily the very things for which such arts are learned, than the complicated and tiresome rules of such disciplines. As if someone, wanting to give rules for walking, warned that the foot at the back should not be raised, unless the foot in front was already seated, and then described in detail how to move the joints of the feet and the hamstrings of the knees. Without a doubt he says the truth, because you cannot do it any other way, but it is easier for men to do this, to realize it when doing it or to understand it when they hear it. Those who cannot walk worry much less about these things that they cannot know through experience. Likewise, the clever man often sees sooner that a conclusion is not valid than he grasps the laws of consequence. The rude person does not see the falsity of the conclusion, but much less the precepts about it. In all these rules, the panorama of truth often delights us more than what they help us when judging and disputing; unless you count in your favor the fact that your wits are exercised with them.

56. The science of numbers, any fool can think of, has not been instituted, but rather investigated and discovered by men. 60. If perhaps those who call themselves philosophers said some truths in accordance with our faith, and especially the Platonists, we must not only fear them, but claim them from them as unjust possessors and apply them to our use. Because just as the Egyptians not only had idols and very heavy burdens from which the people of Israel fled and detested, but also vessels and jewelry of gold and silver and clothing, which the chosen people, upon leaving Egypt, took with them secretly to make better use of them, not by their own authority but by command of God, who made the Egyptians lend, without knowing it, the objects of which they misused; Likewise, all the sciences of the Gentiles not only contain feigned and superstitious fables, and very heavy loads of useless exercises, which each one of us leaving the society of the Gentiles and leading Jesus Christ must hate and detest, but also the liberal sciences, very suitable for the use of truth, contain certain very useful moral precepts and even some truths are found among them concerning the worship of the same one God. All this is like their gold and silver and they did not institute it themselves, but they extracted it from certain mines of divine Providence, which is infused everywhere, whose wealth they perversely and insultingly abused against God to worship demons; When the Christian withdraws with all his heart from the unhappy society of the Gentiles, he must take these goods from them for the just use of the preaching of the Gospel. 8. Not only these, but also those other ambiguities that do not come from punctuation or pronunciation, must be examined in a similar way. Thus, let us see that passage from the Apostle to the Thessalonians: propterea consolati sumus, fratnes, in vobis, for this reason we have taken comfort, brothers, in you. It is doubtful whether "o fratres" is to be understood in the vocative, or "hos fratres" in the accusative, although neither reading is opposed to faith. But the Greek language does not have these two cases equal; That is why consulting the Greek text shows that "fratres" is vocative. If the interpreter had preferred to translate "propterea consolationem habuimus fratres in vobis", he would not have followed the words as closely, but there would be less doubt about the meaning; or if he had added nostri, almost no one would have doubted being vocative, hearing "propterea consolati sumus, fratres nostri, in vobis"; but adding is a more dangerous concession. This is what happened in that sentence of Saint Paul to the Corinthians: quotidie morior, per vestram gloriam, fratres, quam habeo in Christo Jesu, every day I die, brothers, for your glory which I have in Christ Jesus. The translator says like this: "quotidie morior, per vestram juro gloriam", because in the Greek text the word (ne) proper to the oath is found without ambiguity. It is difficult and very rare to find ambiguity in one's own words, as far as the divine books are concerned, that cannot be resolved, or due to the context of the discourse, which shows us the writer's intention; or by the comparison of the translators, or by the examination of the language of the original text.

It narrates past things, announces things to come, and shows things present, but all this is aimed at nourishing and strengthening charity itself, and at conquering and extinguishing greed. 16. I call charity the movement of the soul that leads us to enjoy God for Himself, and ourselves and our neighbor for God. And I call greed the movement of the soul that drags man to the enjoyment of himself and his neighbor and any other corporeal thing without concern for God. What untamed concupiscence or greed does to corrupt its soul and body is called vice or evil; and what he does to harm his neighbor is called wrong or iniquity. Here the two types of sins are evident; but the evils or vices are prior. When these have devastated the soul and reduced it to poverty and misery, it is launched into iniquities or grievances to remove with them the obstacles of vices, or to seek support in order to commit them. Likewise, what charity does for its own benefit is called utility; and what he performs for the benefit of his neighbor is beneficence; But utility precedes beneficence because no one can take advantage of another with what he or she does not have. The more the empire of concupiscence is destroyed, the more that of charity increases.

It would be a very long matter to continue in this way exposing all the tropes one by one; because even the language of the common people goes so far as to use those that are more noticeable because they mean the opposite of what they sound like, as happens with the trope called irony or antiphrasis. Irony through tone indicates what it wants to imply, as when we say to a man who does something wrong, "You did a good job." The antiphrase to mean the opposite does not use the tone of the voice, but rather has its own words, whose origin is of opposite meaning, as the jungle is called lucus (forest) because it lacks light; or it is customary to call a thing meaning the opposite, even if it is not said with contrary words, as, for example, happens when we look for something that is not there in that place, and we are answered, it abounds; or, finally, when by adding words we make the opposite of what we are talking about understood, for example when we say be careful with this one, because he is a good man. What tough guy is there who doesn't talk like that, even if he doesn't know at all what these tropes are and what they are called? Knowledge of them is necessary to resolve the ambiguities of Scripture; because if when taking the words literally the meaning is absurd, we must investigate whether what we do not understand was said with this or that trope. In it he set forth certain seven rules that are like the keys with which the secrets of the divine Scriptures are unlocked. The first one he puts in, he calls "of the Lord and his body"; the second, "of the body of the Lord divided in two"; the third, "of the law and the promises"; the fourth, "of the species and the genus"; the fifth, "of the times"; the sixth, "of the recapitulation"; the seventh, "of the devil and his body." 47. The fourth rule of Tyconius deals with "the species and the genus." He calls it this way wanting to understand by species the part and by genus the whole, of which what he calls species is a part, just as each city is certainly part of the universe. He calls the city a species, and all people a genus. But that subtle distinction taught by dialecticians, who most ingeniously dispute about the difference that exists between the part and the species, must not be applied here. The same rule applies when something similar is found in the divine words, not only of a city, but of each province, nation or kingdom. Because not only of Jerusalem, for example, or of a Gentile city, such as Tyre, Babylon or any other city, something more is said in the Holy Scriptures than is appropriate for it, which would rather suit the universe, but also of Judea, Egypt, Assyria and any other nation, in which there are many cities, but they are not the entire world but parts of it, things are said that surpass the measure and are rather adapted to the universe, whose it is. part, or, as Tyconius says, to the genus of which it is a species. Hence the common people have already come to know this word, species and genus; and thus even the rustics understand in any imperial precept what was ordered in a special way and what was general. This same thing happens when dealing with men, as seen in the words that are said of Solomon exceeding his limits; and rather referring them to Christ or to the Church, of which he is a part, they are clearly understood.

50. He calls the fifth rule established by Tyconius "of the times"; With it it will often be possible to find, or at least conjecture, the amount of time that is danced hidden in the Holy Books. In two ways, he says, this rule is applied: either with the synecdoche figure or with legitimate numbers. By the synecdoche trope the whole is taken for the part or the part for the whole. Thus one evangelist says that what another says after six days happened after eight days, when on the mountain the face of the Lord shone like the sun and his clothes became white as snow in the presence of only three of his disciples. The two things that were said about the number of days cannot be true, unless he who said "after eight days" took the last part of the day in which Christ predicted that this event would be fulfilled, and the first part of the day that took place, for two complete and complete days. And the one who said "after six days" only counted the entire days that intervened between the two incomplete ones. By this way of speaking in which the part is taken for the whole, the question of the resurrection of the Lord is also resolved. Because unless the last part of the day in which he suffered is taken as a full day, that is, adding to it the last night, and if the night in which last part he was resurrected is not taken as a whole day together with the morning of Sunday, the three days and nights that he predicted would be in the heart of the earth cannot occur. 51. Tyconius calls legitimate numbers those that divine Scripture recommends in a more marked way, such as seven, ten, twelve, and others that scholars easily recognize by reading. This kind of number is often put to mean an indefinite time, as I will praise you seven times a day, and it is nothing more than what is said elsewhere: your praise will always be in my mouth. They are the same when multiplied, either by ten, as seventy or seven hundred; and thus the seventy years of Jeremiah can be taken spiritually for all the time in which the Church lives among strangers; pray for themselves, like ten times ten, those who are a hundred; or twelve times twelve, one hundred forty-four.

52. The sixth rule found quite ingeniously in the obscurity of the Scriptures is called "recapitulation" by Tyconius. Some things are presented in such a way as if they continued in the order of time (the previous ones), or are narrated as a continuation of events, when undoubtedly the narration hiddenly refers to previous events that were silenced. If you do not pay attention to this rule, you will fall into some error. Thus in Genesis where it is said: and the Lord God planted paradise in Eden toward the east, and placed in it no man whom he had formed; And God produced even from the earth every tree beautiful and good for food; In such a way it seems that this was said as if it had been done after God had placed man in paradise, being that both facts were briefly commemorated, that is, that God planted paradise and that he placed in it the man whom he formed, he goes back and recapitulating and says what he had omitted, namely, how paradise was planted, God producing from the earth every tree that is beautiful and good for eating. Then, continuing the story, he adds: that the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil were in the middle of paradise. Then he explains that the river with which paradise was watered was divided into four sources, the origin of four rivers; all of which belongs to the formation of paradise. Having finished this narration, he repeated what he had already said and which really followed this, saying: and the Lord God took the man whom he formed, and placed him in paradise, etc. The man was placed there after all these things had been done, as the order itself now demonstrates; and not after the man had been placed there, were the remaining things done, as could be judged from what was said above, if one were not careful to understand there a recapitulation by which one returns to the things that had previously been omitted. 53. Who will not see what the Apostle meant, and how wisely he said it when he wrote: We glory in tribulations knowing that tribulation works patience, patience tests it, hopes tries it, and hope does not deceive us because the love of God has been spread in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us? If someone, so to speak, unindoctrinatedly learned insists on maintaining that the Apostle followed in this place the rules of the art of eloquence, would it not be the ridicule of learned and unlearned Christians? And yet, here we have the figure that the Greeks call (klimax) and in Latin it is called "gradation", because some did not want to call it a "ladder", since it consists of connecting the words or sentences in such a way that they interlock with each other, as we see what happens here, since it links patience with tribulation, with patience the test and with the test hope. Another ornament is also noted here, which is that after each of the phrases or sentences have been pronounced separately, what the Latins call members or subsections and the Greeks (kola) or (kommata), the "circuit" or clause follows, which the Greeks call (periodon) period, whose members are suspended by the speaker until the period is closed with the last one; so here, the first member of those that precede the period is tribulation works patience; the second, patience works the test; and the third is the test of hope. Next follows the period containing three other members, of which the first is hope, it does not deceive us; the second because the love of God has spread in our hearts; and the third by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. All these things and others like them are taught in the art of speaking. Well, just as we do not say that the Apostle followed the rhetorical precepts, we do not deny that eloquence followed wisdom.

The fourth period has two: many indeed boast according to the flesh, I will also boast. The fifth also has two: for you willingly suffer the foolish, being sane. The sixth also has two: for you tolerate if someone reduces you to slavery. Three clauses follow: if someone devours you, if someone takes what (yours), if someone becomes arrogant. Then three other members come: if anyone strikes you in the face, I say it out of dishonor, as if we had been weak. To this is added a period with three other members, to which someone dares, I say it with fatuity, I also dare. From here, three paragraphs that ask questions correspond to three others answering: are they Hebrews? I am also; Are they Israelites? Me too; Are they from the lineage of Abraham? Me too. To the fourth paragraph, also placed in the form of a question, he does not respond with another paragraph, but with the opposition of a member: are they ministers of Christ? I speak like a fool, I above all. This is followed by four other paragraphs, having carefully eliminated the question: in work I exceed them greatly, in prisons much more, in receiving blows excessively, in danger of death many times. Then there is a short period distinguishing with clipped intonation: five times I received from the Jews, this member being the first to whom the second is attached, forty lashes minus one. From here it returns to the paragraphs and they are placed three times saying: three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked. This is followed by a single member: I spent a day and a night in the depths of the sea. Then, with most graceful impetus fourteen paragraphs flow: many times on the roads (I have had) dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the desert, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers. I have gone through all kinds of work and misery, through frequent vigils, through hunger and thirst, through not having food to eat many times, through cold and nakedness.

After these paragraphs he interposes a period of three members, and, apart from these external things, the daily combat over me, the care of all the Churches. To this period he adds two members asking: who gets sick that I don't get sick?

In these things the speech is decorated as with torches with the names of the places of Zion, Samaria, Calanna, Emath the great and Geth of Palestine. Furthermore, the verbs that are attached to these nouns vary beautifully; you are opulent, you trust, come in, go, go down. 18. As a consequence, the approaching arrival of captivity is announced, under an impious king, by adding: those who are separated for the evil day, and are approaching the throne of iniquity. Next he mentions the quality of debauchery: those who sleep on marfd beds, and relax libidinously in their chambers, those who eat the lamb of the flock and the bulls from the middle of the herd. These six members make up three terms of two members each. For it does not say those who are separated for the evil day, those who approach the throne of iniquity, those who sleep on beds of ivory, those who rejoice libidinously in their chambers, those who eat the lamb of the flock and the bulls from the middle of the herd; Even if it were said like this, it would also have been beautiful, because each of the six remaining members would be derived from the same repeated pronoun, each of them ending by suspending the tone of the voice of the speaker. But it was done much more beautifully by joining the same pronoun two by two, developing three sentences; one announcing captivity to them: those who are separated for the evil day, and are approaching the throne of iniquity; the other rebuking his softness: those of you who sleep on ivory beds and indulge libidinously in your chambers; the third, reproaching them for their gluttony: those who eat the lamb of the flock and the bulls from the middle of the herd. So that it is left to the will of the one who recites, either to give final intonation to each member, thus resulting in six, or to suspend with the intonation, the first, third and fifth, joining the second to the first, the fourth to the third, and the sixth to the fifth, thus beautifully forming three two-membered periods; one in which the imminent calamity is evident; another in which their impure bed is revealed to them, and the third in which they are exposed to the sybaritism of the table. 19. Having told them what they, as lustful people, should have heard: you who sing to the sound of the psaltery, he also indicated to others their lack of skill, saying: they judged that like David they had musical instruments. These three sentences are better pronounced if, by leaving the first two members in suspension, the period ends with the third. 20. What is added to all this: and they remained impassive before the crushing of Joseph, whether it is pronounced continuously, so that it forms a single member, or with more grace the voice is suspended after and they remained impassive, continuing after this pause before the crushing of Joseph, thus forming a period of two members, it is always beautiful not to have said, and they remained impassive before the crushing of their brother; but rather to have put Joseph in his brother's place, so that any brother could be signified by the proper name of the one who among his brothers enjoys a distinguished reputation, either for the evils he received from them, or for the goods he returned to them in return. I don't know if in the art of rhetoric we learned and taught? This trope is spoken of, in which any brother with the name of Joseph is implied. How beautiful it is, and how much it impresses the readers who understand it, it is useless to explain it to anyone, if he himself does not notice it. 21. Certainly, many other decorations that concern the norms of eloquence could be noted in this same passage, which we adduced as an example. But the good listener is not so much instructed by the diligent examination of a passage as excited by its enthusiastic delivery. These words were not composed by human industry, but they emanated wisely and eloquently from the divine mind, wisdom not attempting to be followed by eloquence, but eloquence did not depart from wisdom. Because if it is true, as certain very wise and acute men were able to say and observe, that those rules that are learned in the art of oratory would not have been observed and written down, nor would they have been reduced to this body of doctrine, if they had not first been found in the wits of the orators, why should it be admired that they are found in the wits of these men whom He who makes the same wits sent? Therefore let us confess that our canonical authors and doctors are certainly not only wise, but also eloquent, but with such eloquence as was appropriate for such people.

EVEN IF THE DARKNESS OF THE SACRED AUTHORS IS ELOQUENT, IT SHOULD NOT BE IMITATED BY CHRISTIAN AUTHORS.

22. But if we have taken, by way of example, from the sacred authors some passages of eloquence, which are understood without difficulty, nevertheless, we must in no way think that we should imitate them in those passages that they wrote with useful and healthy obscurity in order to exercise and in a certain way sharpen the minds of the readers and at the same time break the boredom and quicken the desire of those who want to learn; or also to hide them from the minds of the wicked so that they may convert to piety or turn away from the mysteries. They spoke in this way so that their successors who understood and explained them correctly would find in the Church of God another grace, certainly unequal, but subsequent to theirs. Therefore the expositors of the sacred authors should not speak in such a way as to suggest themselves, as if they should be explained with equal authority to theirs; Rather, in all their speeches they must try first and foremost to be understood, speaking as much as possible with such clarity that either the person who does not understand must be very rude, or that in the difficulty and subtlety of the things we intend to manifest and explain, our speech is not the cause of it being understood less and with more delay. 24. The diligent desire to give clarity to speech sometimes neglects the most cultured words, and is not concerned with how good they sound, but with how well they declare and explain what is intended to be expressed. That is why a certain author said, when dealing with this type of locution, that there is a certain diligent negligence in it. However, this negligence of this kind strips away the adornment that is not dressed with shame. Although among good teachers there is so much care in teaching, or at least there should be, that if a word, in order to preserve its Latin purity, turns out to be obscure or ambiguous, and in the language of the common people it is said in a way that avoids ambiguity and obscurity, they rather prefer the way in which rustics use it to the way in which the learned express it. And so our interpreters had no qualms about translating: non congregabo conventicle eorum de sanguinibus, I will not congregate or frequent their meetings of "bloods", because they judged that it was appropriate to say in that place in the plural the name "sanguis", which in the Latin language is only used in the singular. 27. So he said, a master of eloquence, and he spoke the truth, that the orator should speak in such a way as to teach, delight and move. And he added later: "teaching is characteristic of necessity, delight of amenity and movement of vichlory." Of these three things, the first that was said, that is, the need to teach, is located in the things we say; the other two in the way they are said. Therefore, he who speaks with the intention of teaching must not judge that he has said what he wanted until it is understood by the one he wanted to teach. For even if he has said what he himself understood, he still must not think that. He said it for those who have not understood him. If you understood him, however he said it, he already said it. If you also want to delight or move those you teach, the way you speak is not indifferent; To achieve this, the way of saying it matters. Just as the audience must be delighted so that they pay attention to what they hear, in the same way they must be convinced so that they are moved to execute what they have heard. He can use great eloquence to move the minds of his listeners, not to teach them what they should do, but to get them to do what they already know must be done. 28. Mine, if they still ignore it, without a doubt they must be taught rather than moved. And it may be that by simply knowing things, they move in such a way that it is no longer necessary to resort to greater efforts of eloquence to move them. However, the latter must be done when necessary, and there is no doubt that it is when, knowing what to do, they do not do it. That is why it was said that teaching is necessary. Men can do or not do what they know, but who will say that they should do what they do not know? For this reason, persuading or moving is not necessary, because it is not always necessary, when the audience gives its assent to the one who teaches or the one who delights. It is said that moving is the work of victory, because it can happen that it is taught and delighted, and yet the listener does not assent. And of what use would the first two efforts of teaching and delight be in such a case, if this third is missing? Nor is delight necessary, since when the truth is made manifest in prayer, what belongs to the office of teaching, it is not done through discourse nor is attention paid to delighting the discourse or the truth, but by itself, because it is truth, it delights already evident. From this it arises that many times false things are also delighting when it is discovered and convinced that they are false; They do not delight because they are false, but because it was made clear that they were false; Delight, then, the reasoning with which this truth was demonstrated.

From the Holy Spirit doctors are made, and by commanding them how and what they should teach? Or rather we must understand that the office of men of teaching even the doctors themselves through the grace of the Holy Spirit must not cease, and that nevertheless also neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase. From this it follows that no one, neither by the work of the holy men themselves, ministers of God, nor by the angels themselves, will learn rightly what belongs to living with God, unless he is made docile by God to God, to whom it is said in the psalm: Teach me to do your will, for You are my God. That is why the Apostle said to Timothy, speaking as a teacher to his disciple: persevere in those things that you learned and were given to you, because you know from whom you learned them. Just as the bodily medicines that men apply to men, only benefit those to whom God gives health, who could heal them without them, since they cannot without God, and yet they are applied; and so laudably that, if this is done by rendering a service, it is counted among the works of mercy or charity, so the teaching aids applied by man will then profit the soul when God makes them profit, who could give a man the gospel without the ministry of men and which is not of men.

In the elevated genre it is always or almost always appropriate that the beginning be of a moderate style, leaving it to the discretion of the speaker to say many things in a simple style even those that could be said in a high style, so that the things that are said in a sublime style appear, in comparison with the others, much higher and become more luminous with the shadows of the former. In any type of style where the difficulties of some issues have to be resolved, it is necessary to make use of clarity and sharpness of wit, which is peculiar and demands for itself the simple style. INTRODUCTION

Regarding the books of Genesis against the Manichaeans, Augustine himself tells us the time of their composition, the reason for their writing and the sense in which he explains the words of Genesis, as the reader can observe in the retraction of these books and in the allusion he makes to them in book VIII, chapter 2, De Genesi ad litteram. There he tells us that he wrote them shortly after his conversion, while he was already in Africa, that is, in the year 388 or 389; that he composed them wanting to refute the follies and errors taught by the Mwmicaeans about the Old Testament, thus coming to its defense; But, not being able to understand at that time how Genesis could be explained literally, he explained figuratively what he could not explain in the proper sense. Book I, which includes the study of chapter 1 of Genesis until verse 3 of chapter 2, begins by telling us that it will use a simple style so that the learned and unlearned can understand it and take advantage of it. After what we could call an introduction, he unravels the meaning of the word principle, and affirms that the cause of creation must only be sought in the will of God. He then tells us about the formless matter, how it was created from nothing and from it all things; of the various names given to this matter; of the creation of light and how darkness is a lack of it; of how God knew this light before making it. From here he goes on to deal with the gathering of waters and the command that God imposed on the earth to produce plants, herbs and fruit trees, explaining why some harmful and fruitless plants were created. He then explains the creation of the stars and how the previous three days could have taken place without the presence of the luminaries. It also deals with the creation of animals and, like the dantas, with the reason why those that seem unnecessary and harmful have been created. It exposes the creation of man; and the dominion he has over the beasts he understands figuratively from the affections of the spirit. It speaks of the rest of the seventh day in an allegorical sense. To finish, compare the •v Ac, 15

seven days to seven ages of the world, giving the reason for the diversity of their duration; and concludes book I by figuratively applying the seven days of creation to man. Book II continues the exposition of chapter 2 of Genesis, from verse 4 to the last verse of chapter 3. It begins by advocating that Genesis be expounded verbatim; But if this cannot be done without falling into error, based on the apostolic authority, which says "omnia in figuris contingebant illis", let it be expressed in a figurative sense. He then affirms that the day of which the Scripture now speaks includes all the time of the first seven, and that the words in the beginning God made the heaven and the earth do not belong to any of the seven days, but to the matter from which all things would be made, that is, to the universal and simultaneous creation; and the seven days recounted immediately after these words were an orderly exposition of the works of God. He explains in a spiritual sense the field and the greenness of the field, and what it means to have not rained on the earth, and what was the source that watered the earth, also indicating that the invisible creature was signified in the name of heaven and earth; the time, in the daytime; and the truth that flooded the soul before sin, at the source. From here he goes on to deal with the formation of man, made of slime and breath; how paradise and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil are to be understood; of the four rivers that represent the four cardinal virtues; of man's work in paradise; the reason the woman was made and also symbolized Adam's dream. It tells how the temptation came to pass; how our first parents hid, the judgment that God had on them and the penalties inflicted for sin. It hints at the meaning of the skin tunics and how the expulsion of our first parents from paradise, the cherub and the flaming sword, is to be understood allegorically. Up to this point he has explained the events of Genesis in a mystical sense. Now it is proposed to make a brief consideration of the prophecy that is also contained in some words of Genesis.

In book VIII From Genesis to the Letter, Saint Augustine writes, in chapter 2, about the books of Genesis against the Manichaeans, the following: «Immediately after my conversion, I wrote two books against the Manichaeans, who not only deceive themselves by interpreting these writings of the Old Testament in a different way than is appropriate, but also blaspheme by rejecting and detesting them outright. I wrote them wanting to instantly refute their follies or direct my mind to seek the evangelical and Christian faith in the writings they hate. And because then it did not occur to me how all the things in these books could be understood in a literal sense, rather it seemed to me that they could not be understood in this sense. they could barely or hardly be; In order not to delay, I explained, as briefly and clearly as I could, what those writings figuratively meant, whose literal meaning I could not then find, since I feared that, terrified by the need for much reading or by the difficulty of the controversy, they would disdain to take it into their hands.

24. And God said: Let the waters produce living reptiles and birds that fly above the earth and under the firmament of heaven, and so it was done: And God made great fish and all animal and teptile life, which the waters produced according to the kind of each one^ and all kinds of winged birds according to the kind of each one. And God saw that they were good, and God blessed them saying: grow and multiply and fill the waters of the womb, and the birds will multiply on the earth; and h<>cha, the evening, was made the morning, the fifth day. Here the Manicheans tend to censure by asking or rather reproaching, why was it written that animals, not only those that live in water, but also those that fly in the air, and all birds that have feathers, were born from water? Let all those who dispute these things know that this nebulous and humid air in which birds fly is usually counted among the waters by very learned men who studied these things with great diligence, because it thickens and becomes denser with the exhalations and vapors of the sea and the land, and in a certain way it is nourished by this same humidity so that it can support the flight of birds; This is why we see that dew falls on calm nights, whose drops we find on the grass at dawn. The mountain in Macedonia called Olympus is said to be of such height that at its summit neither the wind can be felt nor the clouds gather, because it exceeds in height all this humid air in which the birds fly. It is also narrated what has been revealed by men: they used to climb to the top of said mountain every year and I don't know for what reason they were going to sacrifice; that they wrote signs in the dust and the following year they found them intact, which could not happen if that place was exposed to rain or wind; in addition, they say that the thinning of the air that is there does not allow for inspiration and, therefore, they could not stay there for long if they did not apply to

25. And God said: Let the earth produce a living soul according to the kind of four-legged animals, serpents, and beasts of the earth, and so it was done; And God made the beasts of the earth according to their kind, and the grazing animals according to their kind, and all the reptiles according to their kind, and God saw that they were good. The Manichaeans usually raise a question about this by saying: What was the need for God to create such a large number of animals, whether in the water or on the land, since they are unnecessary for man, even more so, since many of them are pernicious and worthy of fear? When they say this, they do not understand how they are all beautiful to their Creator and Artificer, who uses them all for universal government, and to whom they are subject with supreme law. If some ignorant person entered the office of a craftsman and saw an infinite number of instruments there and did not know what they were for, being foolish and senseless, he would judge them superfluous; What's more, if he fell into the nozzle while distracted or injured himself by misusing a spit, he will judge that there are many pernicious and harmful things there; However, the craftsman who knows the use of them laughs at the daring ignorance, and ignoring their insipid words continues the work of his office. And yet, men are so foolish that not daring before a craftsman to reproach what they do not know, but when they see those instruments they judge them necessary and made for specific uses, of this world that announces God as Creator and Governor, they dare to censure many things, whose causes they do not see, and in the works and means of the Omnipotent Artificer they want to pretend to know what they do not know. 26. If these charlatans and inept people would think this through, they wouldn't bore us; Considering so many small and great beauties, they would praise the Artificer God from all corners of the world; and since in contemplating these things reason is never damaged in any part, as perhaps the carnal sense is sometimes damaged, do not attribute it to the imperfection of the things themselves, but to the condition of our mortality. True, all animals are for us either harmful or superfluous or useful; The Manichaeans have nothing to say against the tools; Of the pernicious ones we will say that they either punish us or worry us or frighten us so that we do not love this life subject to so many dangers and work, but rather the other, better one where supreme happiness reigns, which we will achieve with the merits of our piety; Of the superfluous ones, why worry about them? If you dislike what is not useful, please like what is not harmful; If they are not necessary for our house, however, through them the integrity of the universe is completed, which is much more excellent and exalted than our house, the Lord governs this house of the world much better than each one of us governs his own. Therefore, use useful things, protect yourself from harmful things and don't worry about superfluous things. However, as you see the order, measure and number in all of them, look for the Creator; for you will find no other except him who is the highest measure, the supreme number and the most perfect order, that is, God, of whom it was said with absolute truth: that he arranged all things in measure, number and weight; So perhaps you will get more fruit when you praise God in the smallness of an ant than when you cross the river on the back of a tall donkey. On this question the Manichaeans tend to shout to the heavens with vain and senseless speeches, and mock us because we believe that man was made in the image and likeness of God, since they pay attention to our bodily figure and the unfortunate people ask: Does God have noses and teeth and beards and entrails and everything else that is necessary in us? Rightly, then, they say that supposing such things in God is ridiculous, nay, it is impious to believe it; Therefore, they deny that man was created in the image and likeness of God. To which we will respond that, when God wants to make himself understandable to the children who listen to him, these members are mentioned in divine Scripture, not only in the books of the Old Testament but also in those of the New, since in them they speak of God's eyes, his ears, his lips and his feet, and it is announced that the Son sits at the right hand of God the Father; and the Lord himself says: do not swear by heaven because it is the seat of God, nor by the earth because it is his footstool, and he also says of himself that with the finger of God he cast out demons. But all those who spiritually grasped the meaning of the divine Scripture understood that by these names are not to be understood the bodily members, but the spiritual powers, as when the Apostle speaks of the helmet or the shield or the sword or many other similar things. First of all, it must be said to these heretics that they shamelessly slander such words from the Old Testament, since they observe that the same words are also used in the New, but perhaps they do not see them because when they dispute they become blind. 28. But know that in the Catholic Islands the faithful devotees do not believe that God is defined by bodily form. What is said that man was made in the image of God is understood from the inner man where reason and intelligence reside, by which he dominates the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky, and all the animals and wild beasts, and all the earth and all the reptiles that crawl on the earth; because when he had said let us make man in our image and likeness, he then added: and let him dominate the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky, etc., so that we would understand that he had not said that man was made in the image of God by the body, but by that power by which he subdues the beasts.
For all other animals are subject to man, not because of the body, but because of the understanding that we have and which they lack; although our body has also been formed in such a way.

29. The Manichaeans sometimes say: How did man receive dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the sky and over all animals and wild beasts, when we see that many wild beasts kill men, and that many birds harm our property, which we wish to either scare away or catch and most of the time we cannot? According to this, in what way have we received dominion over them? Based on these figurative locutions, those who knew this allegorical way of speaking, without any difficulty, resolve many questions of divine Scripture. Such locutions also abound in the ordinary custom of speaking; For example, when we say that the day is happy we say it because we have had a happy time; We say that the cold is lazy, because with it we are lazy; We also say "blind pit" because we do not see it; We say "polished language" because the words chosen make it that way; and, finally, we say that the weather is serene and free from the elements because in it we are free of any disturbance. It was said, then, that God rested from all his works, which were exceedingly good, because in him we will rest from all our labors if we work well, and because also our own good works must be attributed to Him, who calls us, who shows us the path of truth, who asks us to want and who supplies us with the strength to fulfill what he commands.

This virtue of prudence surrounds the entire earth that possesses gold, diamonds and emeralds, that is, a doctrine that contains the teachings of living, which, as if purified by fire from all earthly filth, shines like the purest gold and contains within itself the truth that is not defeated by any falsehood, just as the brilliance of the diamond is not defeated by the night, and carries in itself the eternal life that is represented in the perennial greenery of the emerald because It never loses its vigor. The river that surrounds Ethiopia, an extremely warm and fiery land, means the courageous and diligent strength at the climax of the action. They say: why did God make man knowing that he would sin? Because he could also do many good things from sin, directing it according to the standard of his divine justice, and also because man's sin harms God in no way. If there had been no sin, there would have been no death either, and if he sinned we have other mortals correct themselves because of sin.
