Finally, since the dispute between the Manichaeans and us is about religion, this religious question is posed thus: what should be thought with all reverence for God, since we cannot doubt that the human race is involved in the misfortune of sin? They say that the nature of God is in misery; We deny it and say that only the nature that God made out of nothing is found in misery, and that, without anyone forcing it, it rushed into such a state by its own will to sin. They say that the nature of God is compelled by God himself to do penance for his sins; We deny it, and say that only the nature that God made from nothing, after it sinned, is obliged to do penance for the sins committed. They say that God's nature is forgiven by God himself; We deny it, but we say that the nature that God made from nothing, if it turns itself away from sin and turns towards its God, receives forgiveness of its sins. They say that the nature of God is mutable by necessity; We deny it, and say that the nature that God made from nothing was changed by his own will. They say that the nature of God is harmed by the sins of others; We deny it, and we say that no nature is harmed by other people's sins, except by its own, and we add that God is of such goodness, of such justice, of such incorruption, that He neither sins nor harms anyone who does not want to sin, nor does He allow Him to sin.

Augustine's first exposition of Genesis in the literal sense only includes the first twenty-six verses of Genesis. He undertook this task in order to test his strength in the laborious effort of explaining it to the letter. In the year 388 he tried against the Manichaeans and could not; Now, in 393, he insists again, but faced with the enormous weight that was placed on him, not being able to bear it, he left it, writing only one book and incomplete, as he tells us in the retraction he made of it. Making a complete review of the content of this book, as well as of those that make up this volume, is an impossible thing, because the subject matter is such, so many issues it touches on, the sentences are sometimes so concise, and the philosophical and theological substance is so profound, that unless the work is read in its entirety, the reader will not fully realize its content. When we say, then, that these three names, matter of the world, formless matter, fabricable matter, are denominations of a single thing, we insinuate that the first of them fits very well with that of heaven and earth, to the second that of darkness, confusion, depth, darkness; and the third was that of adaptability on which the Spirit of the craftsman was brought to work. 16. And the Spirit of God was carried over the water. It was not borne in the way that water bears oil; or the earth to the water, that is, as if it supported it. If we are to take examples from visible things to understand this, we will say that this is how the Spirit of God was borne, as the light of the sun or the light of the moon, which illuminates the earth, is borne by the terrestrial bodies, not being contained or enclosed in them, but rather the sky contains it, and is borne by them; We must also avoid believing that the Spirit of God was carried over matter, occupying places. It was carried by a certain active and operational power so that what it bore was done and manufactured; in the way that the will of the craftsman is carried out on the wood or on any other material destined to make something out of it, or also how the members of the body carry out the will that mobilizes them to act. This similarity, however, being of greater excellence than any body, has hardly any place and is almost of no use in clarifying for us the most excellent power of the Spirit of God, to whose virtue the matter of the world is subject to act in it; but we find no similarity more clear and appropriate to evince the matter treated than that of these things, which can in any way be understood by men.

Therefore, in these intellectual investigations we must take into account that precept of Scripture: those of you who bless God exalt Him as much as you can, since He is even higher. This was written so that we understand in this passage by the Spirit of God the Holy Spirit, whom we venerate in the ineffable and immutable Trinity.

The Spirit of God can also be understood in another sense; Judging it to be a vital creature, in which this visible world with all its bodies was contained and moved, to which the omnipotent God granted a certain power that would serve to act on those things that were produced. Are not the things created by Him from God? Certainly so, for when speaking of the earth it was said: The earth belongs to God and all the things that it contains; and speaking of the universal set of beings it is said: Oh, Lord, who loves souls, all things are yours. 18. A third opinion can originate from this word spirit: to judge that under the name of spirit the element air is expressed, so that the four elements of which this visible world is composed would be called here, namely, sky, earth, water and air; not because they existed separately and ordered, but because in the still formless confusion of that matter, they were, nevertheless, predetermined to be created from it, to whose confusion and formlessness the name of abyss and darkness was given. 19. And God said: Let there be light, and there was light. We should not believe that when he said God, let there be light, he said it with a voice emitted by the lungs, teeth and tongue, but rather that it was ineffably said, let there be light. Carnal would be such thoughts, and to understand carnally is a death. We may ask (excluding such impiety, namely, that the Word of God the Only Begotten Son is a voice emitted, like our word), whether this thing that was said was said by the Only Begotten Son, or the Only Begotten Son is the same thing that was said, because the word of God, by whom all things were created, is called the Word. The Word of God by whom all things were made did not even begin to be. nor will it cease to be: begotten without beginning, he is coeternal with the Father. Therefore, if what was said, let there be light, began to be said and ended being said, we understand that this word was said by the Son before it itself was the Son, however, this was also said ineffably. Let no carnal idea creep into the soul and torment the holy and spiritual thought; It is a reckless and dangerous opinion to understand, in the proper sense, that in the nature of God something begins and ceases to exist; tolerable opinion in children and in the carnal, not so that they remain in it, but so that it may be like the beginning of a resurrection to the fullness of the truth. Everything that is said about God, which begins or ends, is in no way to be understood as happening in the nature of God, but in His creature, which is subject to Him in a wonderful way. 20. And God said: Let there be light. Is it perhaps the light that hurts these carnal eyes or some other hidden light that we are not allowed to contemplate with the eyes of the body? And if this is hidden, will it be corporeal and perhaps expand through the highest parts of the world? Or is it incorporeal like that of the soul, to which belongs the examination of what must be avoided and what must be desired through the bodily senses, which the souls of beasts do not lack either? Or is it the most excellent one that manifests itself when reasoning and that is the beginning of everything that has been created? Whatever light is meant in this word we must believe that it has been made and created, and that it is not that light by which the Wisdom of God itself shines, which is not created but begotten by. INTRODUCTION

If Augustine had written only this work, he could rightly be called a genius, since such is the accumulation of questions he studies on theology, philosophy, mysticism, natural sciences, mathematics, astrology, etc., when investigating the literal meaning of the first three chapters of the Old Testament, that not without reason one is left in awe of his genius and ingenuity. But since he not only wrote this of the first magnitude, but, among others, the Confessions, the City of God, the Treatise on the Gospel of Saint John, On the Trinity, plus a hundred other treatises on various issues, he can rightly be called the universal Genius. This work is the fourth that comes out of his hands on the Gt'nesis exhibition. He composed the first against the Manichaeans, explaining Genesis in an allegorical sense, because at that time he could not carry it out in a historical sense; Later he tried, but had to give it up, writing only one book, and not a complete one, because he saw that it was too heavy a job for him. In the year 400, upon finishing his Confessions, he added to them three books on Genesis, exposing it in an allegorical sense. In the first he studies the first verse of the Old Testament, indicating how the words beginning, heaven and earth can be understood; and after answering those who ask what God did before time, he speaks at length about memory and time. He dedicates book II to verse 2: understanding the spiritual creature by heaven, and the corporeal creature by earth, he explains what formlessness consisted of, and ends the book by talking about the various meanings that can be given to Scripture, as long as they are true, when we do not know the meaning intended by the author. In book III he studies verse 3: Let the light be erased, what do you understand by illumination of the spirit creature?!; continues with the firmament, the congregation of waters, the creation of herbs, lights and animals, explaining everything in a spiritual sense applied to man; It ends with the creation of man in the image and likeness of God, for Augustine this image and likeness is the renewal of man in God. Around the year 401 he undertook the task of exposing Genesis again, which he did in a complete manner.

And, therefore, it may still be asked when God created these visible forms and qualities of the earth and water, because in none of the six days is this expressed. If he did it before any day, as it was written, before the enumeration of these first days, in the beginning God made the heaven and the earth, then we will understand by the word "earth" the already constituted form of the earth; and the previously mentioned waters spread over it, with the visible and proper form that they now have. And from what the Scripture goes on to say: the earth was invisible and formless and darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was carried over the waters, we must judge that the matter was not absolutely formless, but that the earth and the water, being without light, which had not yet been made, had already clearly created their qualities. And thus we will understand that the earth was called invisible, because being covered by waters it could not be seen, although there was someone who could contemplate it; and that it was called shapeless or disordered because it was not separated from the sea and bordered by beaches and adorned with its own animals and fruits. The angels do not follow the method that we follow to know wisdom, in such a way that they perceive and understand the invisible things of God through the things that were created, but from the moment they were created they enjoy the holy and pious contemplation of the very eternity of the Word, and, therefore, despising created things, only according to what they see internally, they either approve the good acts or disapprove the bad ones. Understand this well, that the name firmament does not force us to believe that the sky is still. If the truth convinced us that the sky is still, the course of the stars would not prevent us from believing it. Well, those who sought these things out of curiosity and leisure found that, if the sky does not move, if the stars move, all the things that happen and are noticed in the revolutions of the stars can very well happen.

By these words he only wanted to hint at the formlessness of corporeal matter, choosing to call it words that were more common than obscure. However, if a rude understanding does not understand how Scripture separates matter and form in words, let it try to separate these two things in time, as if the matter had first existed, and by interposing a space of time, the form had been added afterwards, notwithstanding that God created these two things at the same time determining the matter and the form, of which formlessness, as I said, the Scripture spoke with the usual words of earth or water. Although the earth and water have existence with the qualities with which we see them, nevertheless, due to their easy decomposition, they are closer to that formlessness than the celestial bodies.

Some believed that from this word (breath) it was deduced that the soul was something of the substance of God, that is, of the same nature as He is; and they affirmed this because when man blows he throws something of his nature into the breath. To these, above all, we warn them that this sentence must be rejected, because it is opposed to the Catholic faith. We Catholics believe that the nature and substance of God is the same Trinity, which many believe and few understand, and which is absolutely immutable. But who does not know that the nature of the soul can be changed for the worse or for the better? Therefore, believing that the soul and God are of the same substance is a sacrilegious opinion; Well, what else is believed with this, if not that God is also mutable? Therefore, it must be believed and also understood and in no way doubted, what right reason affirms, that the soul comes from God, as a thing created by Him, not as a nature of Him, whether He created it or in any way produced it. Another was also built on the land that symbolizes the first one; and that Sara and Hagar, although they symbolized the two Testaments, were nevertheless also two women; and that Christ who waters us through the passion of the cross with the spiritual water of grace, was also a stone, the one who, wounded with the rod, flowed water for the thirsty people, of whose stone it would be said 'later the stone was Christ. All of these things meant something other than what they were, even though they existed in reality. Thus, when the historian related it, it was not his figurative way of speaking, but a clear relationship of present events that also included future things. There was, then, a tree of life, just as there was a stone that was Christ. However, God did not want man to live in paradise without mysteries of spiritual things, represented by material things. Therefore, man had his food in the other trees, and in that of life also a sacrament, because like Christ with a stone that flows water for the thirsty, this tree represented the wisdom of which it was said: It is a tree of life for those who embrace it. It is right that the name is imposed on a thing, which exists before, to be a figure of another; Thus, He is a lamb that is sacrificed at the Passover, and yet it was a figure, not only in terms of the name, but also in terms of its sacrifice, because it cannot be said that that lamb was not a lamb, it was certainly a lamb that was sacrificed and eaten, and, nevertheless, with that fact another fact is prefigured. This is not the same as the fatted calf, which upon the youngest son's return to his father's house, was sacrificed to celebrate the banquet, because here the narrative is figurative, and there are no things that have happened in reality symbolizing others. This was not narrated by the evangelist, but by the Lord himself. The evangelist says it was narrated by the Lord. Therefore, what the evangelist writes is a fact, that is, that the Lord said such words, but the Lord's own narration was a parable, of which it is never required that the3 words uttered in these discourses correspond to real facts. Christ is certainly the stone anointed by Jacob and the cornerstone that was rejected by those who built, but that stone and union were also real, but this stone is nothing more than a figure. The narrator spoke of the former as things previously past, and of the latter, predicting future things.

To this I add that although that tree offered bodily nourishment, it nevertheless provided such virtue that it secured the man's body in permanent health; not as giving it another food, but proceeding from some hidden movement of health. Common bread also had a nutritional power greater than ordinary, since with just one God sustained a man for forty days without feeling hungry. Do we doubt that God could have given man, through the food of some tree that contained a benefit of the highest significance, the gift by which his body would not become worse due to illness or age, or reach decomposition through death, when He gave the same human food the admirable condition of being replaced in fragile vessels, short of flour and oil, in such a way that from now on these substances would not be lacking? Now it may be that someone from the guild of charlatans will appear and say that God should have done such miracles in our times and lands, but in paradise he should not have done them: as if raising man from the dust or forming woman from the side of man, which was done there, were no greater miracle than now raising the dead.

It was appropriate, therefore, that something should be prohibited to the man placed under the dominion of the Lord God, so that in this way his obedience would be the virtue that deserved the possession of his Lord; whose obedience I can say with all truthfulness that it is the only virtue for every rational creature that works under the dominion of God; and the first and greatest of all vices is pride, which leads man to ruin by making him use his freedom to the detriment of the reverence due to his God, which vice is called disobedience. Therefore, the tree was not evil, but it was called the tree of knowledge of the science of good and evil, because if after the prohibition a man ate from it, the future transgression of the precept would occur in you, through which he would learn in the experience of punishment the difference that existed between the good of obedience and the evil coming from disobedience. Therefore, this log was not called a tree in a figurative sense, but the real tree should be taken as the one to which the name of the discernment of good and evil was imposed, not because of the fruit or the apple that grew from it, but because of the reality that would follow if it were touched against what was forbidden by God.

13. A river flowed from Eden which watered paradise, and from there it divided into four. Of these one is called Phison and this is the one who travels throughout the land of Evilath, where there is gold, and the gold of that land is good, there are also diamonds and emeralds there. The name of the second is Geon, this is the one that crosses the entire land of Ethiopia. The third river is called, Tigris, this is the one that flows towards the Assyrians. The fourth is the Euphrates. Regarding these rivers I will only endeavor to demonstrate that they are true rivers, and that those that did not exist were not figuratively named, as if only these names meant something else, since these rivers are very well known in the regions through which they flow, and very connoted for the majority of men. Therefore, I judge that it is not meaningless, but rather that it warns us of something, and of something very important, that from the beginning of this divine book which begins like this: In the beginning God made heaven and earth, until the Lord God was never written to him, but only God. Now, upon arriving at where it is said that he placed man in paradise and commanded him to work and guard under a precept, this is how the Scripture speaks: And the Lord God took the man, whom he formed and placed in paradise to work and guard him. He does not say this because God was not the Lord of the creatures mentioned above, but since this was not written for the sake of angels, nor for any other creature, but only for man, he did not want to put it before, but when he arrived at the placement of man in paradise to work and guard him, in order to warn him to what degree it was more necessary for him to have God as Lord, that is, to live obediently under his dominion, than to wantonly abuse his own freedom. Therefore, now it is not said as in the other things that were written above: God took the man that he made, but the Lord God took the man that he made and put him in paradise to work him, so that he would be righteous, and to keep him to be safe under God's own dominion, which is not useful for Him, but for us. Certainly He does not need our servitude, but we need to be under His dominion so that He can work and guard us. Therefore, He alone is the true Lord, because we do not serve Him for His usefulness, but for our benefit and health. If He needed us, He would not be the true Lord, since He would remedy his need through us, under which He would appear as a servant. No wonder the Psalmist says: I said to the Lord, you are my God, because you do not need my goods. But neither should we dwell on what we said, that He serves us for our usefulness and health, as if we expected something else from Him apart from Himself, which is the highest usefulness and health. Therefore, without profit for Him, we love Him according to what the psalm sings: It is good for me to be united to God.

4. The serpent was the wisest of all the beasts that were on the earth, which the Lord God had created. When translating it was said to be the most prudent or, as many Latin codices write, the wisest; but not in the sense of perfection as it is customary to take wisdom, whether from God or the angels or the rational soul, but as if it were said that bees or ants are wise because of the works they do imitating wisdom in them. Although it could certainly be said that this serpent was the wisest of all beasts, not by virtue of its irrational soul, but by the alien spirit it possessed, that is, by the devil; For no matter how much the prevaricating angels, in reward for their perversity and arrogance, have been degraded by being stripped of their heavenly seats, nevertheless in nature they are more excellent, due to their eminent reason, than all beasts. It is not surprising that the devil, by means of his natural impulse, filling the body of the serpent and mixing his spirit with hers, in the same way that he usually occupies that of the omens, would have made it the wisest of all the beasts that live with an irrational and living soul. By abuse of the name, an evil action is called wisdom, just as the word cunning is also applied to a good act, whereas, speaking properly and using the word with righteousness, in the Latin language those who act laudably are called wise, and the wicked are called clever. Hence, not a few, as we will find in many codices, using the vulgar use of the Latin language, transferred not the word itself, but rather the meaning, and chose to say that this snake was the most cunning of all beasts and not the wisest. Whatever property the Hebrew language has in this, namely, whether the word wise can be said and understood by applying it not abusively, but properly to evil, let those who know it thoroughly say. 18. In this work it should only be treated, based on Scripture, what should be said about the devil. First of all, he asks himself whether from the beginning of the world, delighting in his own power, he separated himself from that company and love by which the angels who enjoy the presence of God are blessed. Or if for some time he remained united with the holy congregation of angels, being himself just and blessed with them; for many say that he was cast out of heaven because he was envious of man made in the image of God. But envy does not precede, but rather follows, pride, since envy is not the cause of pride, but, on the contrary, pride is the foundation of envy. Since pride is the inordinate love of one's own excellence, and envy is the hatred of the happiness of others, it is immediately obvious where the latter comes from. Anyone who loves his own excellence either hates his peers because they are equal to him, or his inferiors so that they do not become equal to him, or his superiors because he cannot become what they are. Then, being conceited, one becomes envious, but by not envying, one becomes arrogant.

Every deprivation diminishes, and thus, from the moment that anyone wants to stand out through pride, he falls into anguish and misery, since from common love it leads him to his own and fatal love of himself. HOW I JUDGE WHAT WAS WRITTEN ABOUT MOSES SHOULD BE UNDERSTOOD

55. As we read in the Exodus, Moses desired to see God in the substance that he has and by which he is God, without the consumption of a corporeal creature that is presented to the mortal and carnal senses, that is, not as he saw him on the mountain and saw him in the tabernacle, and, therefore, not in spirit under figures similar to bodies, but in his very essence, insofar as it can be understood by the rational and intellectual creature, dispensing with all sense of the body and all representative figures that impress the spirit. Thus it is written: If I have found favor in your sight, show yourself to me as you are, so that I may see you. But since shortly before it was read that the Lord spoke to Moses face to face as he usually speaks to his friend, it follows that up to the present this speaking face to face was not God manifesting himself in his essence, but he only felt what he saw, and desired what he did not see, as confirmed by what was written below, because when God said immediately: You found grace before me and I keep you present before everyone, Moses answers: Show me your beauty. On this occasion he also receives a figurative response, of which there is no reason to speak at length now, when he said to him: You cannot see my face and live, because a man will not see my face and live, and he continues saying: Here is a place next to me; Stand on the rock so that when My Majesty passes by, placing you inside the cave of the rock and covering the entrance with my hand as I pass, I deflect it a little and then you will see the back of my face, because you will not see my face. Since Scripture does not continue to speak of this, and also narrates the event in a corporal sense, it sufficiently demonstrates that this was said figuratively of the Church. All the things that are said here are perfectly adapted to the Church, and thus, the place that is next to God is the Church, which is a temple of Him, built on stone. However, if Moses had not deserved to see the beauty of God so desired and longed for by him, God would not have said in the book of Numbers to Aaron and Mary, his brothers: Hear my words; If there is a prophet of the Lord among you, he will know me in vision and I will speak to him in dreams, but like my servant Moses there is no other equally faithful among all my people; face to face I will speak to him in my being and not in riddles, and he will see the splendor of the Lord. If anyone asks why it is necessary for the souls of the deceased to take on their own bodies through the resurrection, when they too can receive perfect blessedness without them, I will tell him that it raises an extremely difficult question and more extensive than what can be treated here. I will note, however, that it is in no way to be doubted that the mind of man, taken from the bodily senses, in this life, and after death, before resurrection, when it has put off the flesh and abandoned the bodily likenesses, cannot see the immutable substance of God in the same way as the holy angels see it, either due to an occult cause or because it has in itself a certain natural inclination to govern its body, by which He delays in a certain way in putting all his attention on that supreme heaven, during the time he is without his body; but once he obtains it through the resurrection, he will rest from this appetite and will be completely free to see God. As long as the body is in such a condition that its government is difficult and burdensome for the soul, as is the condition of this flesh that is corrupted and overburdens the soul, because it has its origin in the spread of sin, much more does the soul depart from that vision of the supreme heaven. Therefore it was necessary to tear it away from the senses of the flesh itself so that heaven could be shown to it in a way that could be understood. But when this body is no longer animal, but through future transformation receives the spiritual form, equal to that of the angel, it will possess the perfect state of its nature.

69. Without a doubt the blessed will have these three types of visions in heaven, without any error that makes them approve one thing for another, neither in the corporal visions nor in the spiritual ones, much less in the intellectual ones, with which they enjoy in a special way, because they are present and visible to their soul with much more evidence and clarity than these corporeal forms that now join us and we touch with the senses of the flesh, to which many give themselves up in such a way that They judge that only they exist, and they think that everything that is not them is non-existent. The wise men behave in such a way in these bodily visions that, however, although they see them before their eyes, they are more certain of those others that they see in any way through intelligence without corporeal forms and without corporeal images, although they are not capable of seeing these visions with the mind, as they are capable of seeing bodies with the senses of the flesh. As for the holy angels who preside over corporeal things, in order to administer and judge them, we will say that if they do not tend toward corporeal things, becoming familiar with them as if they were their proper object, they nevertheless contemplate in their spirit the representative images of things, and administer them in such a way and with such power that they can transform them in the spirit of man by revealing them to him. Furthermore, they also contemplate the immutable substance of the Creator in such a way that, through the vision and love that it inspires in them, they put it before all things, and judge other beings according to it; They pay attention to it when they act, and everything they do is carried out under its direction. Finally, although the Apostle was taken from the senses of the flesh and transported to the third heaven and paradise, he nevertheless lacked, in order to have a perfect and absolute knowledge of the things that angels possess, to know whether that vision was with the body or without the body. This will certainly not be lacking when the souls, having received the bodies in the resurrection of the dead, this corruptible body puts on incorruptibility, and this mortal body puts on immortability. Then everything will be evident, there will be no falsehood,

70. I know certainly that many of those who explained the holy Scriptures before me are praised in the Catholic faith, and that they so expounded the third heaven of which the Apostle speaks, that they wanted to see in this passage the differences that exist between the "corporal, animal, and spiritual" visions, and that the Apostle was caught up to contemplate with excellent evidence that kind of incorporeal things that spiritual men put before everything and long to enjoy in this life. I already explained sufficiently, at the beginning of this book, why I preferred to call spiritual and intellectual what they called "animal and spiritual."
